titre: History's First Spam Message Was Typed by Hand
accroche: On May 3, 1978, a Digital Equipment marketing manager sends the first known spam to about 400 addresses, one by one, over ARPANET.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 3, 1978, an engineer at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) named Carl Gartley types, one by one, into the recipient field of an electronic message, the addresses of about four hundred people connected to ARPANET, the network that precedes the Internet. He acts on behalf of Gary Thuerk, the company's marketing manager, who wants to announce two open house events, in Los Angeles and San Mateo, where DEC is showing off its new DECSYSTEM-20 computers.

## A gesture with no tool built for it

Nothing in the electronic mail of 1978 is designed for this kind of sending. ARPANET's mail software is meant for writing to one person, or a few, not to hundreds at once: there is no mailing list, no blind copy, only a field where each address is typed by hand. To reach the audience targeted by the announcement, Thuerk and Gartley have no choice but to copy out the whole list, one address after another.

The message, brief and written in capital letters, simply announces the two presentations. But the ARPANET of 1978 is not a commercial space: it is a research network funded by the US Department of Defense, reserved for universities and contracted laboratories. An advertising message is, to users of the time, an act out of place, almost an intrusion.

## The reaction came before the word

The reaction is almost unanimously negative: several recipients complain, and an ARPANET administrator calls Thuerk to make him promise not to do it again. The word “spam” does not yet exist to describe this kind of sending; it will not take hold until the 1990s, with the Internet's spread to the general public. Thuerk, for his part, will later say the operation brought DEC about thirteen to fourteen million dollars in sales, a figure that remains his own, unverified by any independent source. He says he never did it again.

The first mass commercial message in the history of the Internet was thus born neither of hacking nor of a dedicated tool: it was born of a workaround, a list typed by hand on a network that was not built for it, thirteen years before the word to name it would exist. The term would only take hold once the Internet opened to the public, in the 1990s, when Thuerk's isolated act became an industrial practice, then a problem email systems would have to learn to filter.

repere.texte: The advertising message sent on May 3, 1978, by Gary Thuerk, of Digital Equipment Corporation, to about 400 ARPANET addresses, is today considered the first spam in the history of the Internet, thirteen years before the word came into use to describe it.
repere.source: NPR, “At 30, Spam Going Nowhere Soon,” 2008; Smithsonian Magazine, 2017

carte.punch: History's first spam message was typed one address at a time, by hand
carte.idee: On May 3, 1978, a Digital Equipment Corporation engineer types, one by one, the addresses of 400 people on ARPANET to announce two commercial open houses. The word spam would not exist for another thirteen years, but the reaction is already unanimously negative.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Details Carl Gartley's role and the technical context of ARPANET in 1978.

quiz.question: Why did Gary Thuerk and his team have to type every address by hand, in 1978?
choix: Because ARPANET's mail system had neither mailing lists nor blind copies
Because Thuerk wanted to personally check each recipient before sending
Because the software refused to send more than ten messages per minute
Because ARPANET's email addresses changed every week
quiz.explication: ARPANET's email in 1978 could only be addressed to one person, or a few, at a time: there was no mailing list and no blind copy, which forced Thuerk and his colleague Carl Gartley to copy out each address one by one.
